DEMONSTRATION PROBLEMS To explore the use of these expressions for the critical pressure required for pipeline collapse, this section details a representative set of pipes for a natural gas network. The expressions provided in section 2 are then applied to the pipes to estimate failure pressures for each of the three main failure modes: cross-section yielding, cross-section buckling, and longitudinal buckling. The demonstration then continues with the ground ranges required to achieve specific overpressure and dynamic pressure values for a selection of nuclear blasts from 1 to 1000 kT. Comparison of these values with the failure pressures yield approximations of how far from the given nuclear detonations pipeline collapse can be expected. 3.1. Representative pipelines The following six pipes were selected as representative of key parts of a gas distribution network: 1. Main pipeline, 36” diameter and .75” thick, buried at a 30” depth 2. Main pipeline, 36” diameter and .75” thick, above ground 3. Lateral pipeline, 12” diameter and .33” thick, buried at an 18” depth 4. Lateral pipeline, 12” diameter and .33” thick, above ground 5. Compressor station pipeline, 3” diameter and .167” thick, above ground 6. Processing Plant pipeline, 6” diameter and .25” thick, above ground This work assumes a set of values in order to provide the information needed for computation of critical collapse pressures. These assumptions include the following:  Design guidelines [6] indicate that gas pipelines can have operating internal pressures of between 100 and 1500 psi. This work assumes a 200 psi internal working pressure.  Pipes in this study use A36 steel, with a 29,000 ksi modulus and a 36 ksi yield. They are also nearly perfectly round, with only a .001 ratio between the pipe deflection and the outer diameter.  Soils in this study use a 1.5 grams per cubic centimeter density, a 7 ksi elastic modulus, and a 25° failure slope, corresponding to a medium dense sand mixture, or a loose sand and gravel mix.
